items.title: Grocers sell bananas at 66 cents a pound to lure you in. What could be the strongest El Niño on record is testing that
items.summary:
Bananas are one of the cheapest groceries at supermarkets. Americans paid just 66 cents per pound of the yellow fruit in October, compared to $2.10 for tomatoes and $2.14 for lemons, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data . But they’re about to get more expensive thanks to El Niño, which causes either wetter-or-drier-than-usual conditions for banana growers thousands of miles away. 

Less rainfall stunts bananas’ growth, which can yield harvest losses of up to 65% , and too much rainfall waterlogs the soil and incubates fungal and bacterial disease , which also reduces yields. And this year’s El Niño could be historically destructive, with about a 60% chance of the event exceeding previous El Niños dating back to 1950. 

The threat is part of why growers are asking wholesalers for more money for the fruit—and getting it—which could test bananas’ status as a loss leader for grocery stores. Costa Rica’s National Banana Corporation has recommended increasing the minimum export price of bananas by nearly 10% for next year, citing climate-driven productivity losses, a stronger currency and higher costs after seven years of no changes. Fairtrade International also approved a 5.6% increase in its average minimum prices for banana growers starting in January, citing El Niño as one of the reasons.

Francisco Martin-Rayo, CEO and cofounder of agricultural commodity price and climate risk forecaster Helios AI, told Fortune the El Niño weather extremes are “dramatically higher” and could destroy harvests next year.

“A lot of harvests will be ruined, 1,000%,” Martin-Rayo said.…
items.t: Grocers sell bananas at 66 cents a pound to lure you in. What could be the strongest El Niño on record is testing that

items.title: Disney’s sports profit jumped 53% as it bets on live games. It also wants $3 billion in cost cuts
items.summary:
Disney’s next growth era is being built around live games. ESPN will produce its first Super Bowl on Feb. 14, 2027; every Disney+ subscriber in the U.S. can stream it, and the network has just locked up exclusive rights to an expanded College Football Playoff.

For now, the bet is paying off. Disney’s Sports segment posted $4.6 billion in revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter, up 16% from a year earlier, while operating income jumped 53%. But Disney is pairing that push with a plan to cut about $3 billion in annual costs by fiscal 2029, signaling how far it is moving away from the traditional TV business that once paid for everything.

That tension defines the strategy. Disney, No. 44 on the 2026 Fortune 500 , is raising its content budget, with sports rights a major line item, while trimming the rest of the company to fund growth.

Why ESPN has become central to Disney’s strategy 

ESPN offers something most streaming libraries can’t: appointment viewing. Fans watch live, in large numbers, and advertisers pay a premium to reach them.

Disney deepened that advantage in January, when ESPN closed its acquisition of NFL Network and NFL Fantasy, along with the rights to distribute the RedZone channel to cable and satellite operators. In exchange, the NFL took a 10% stake in ESPN. Disney now holds an effective 72% interest in the network, according to its fiscal fourth-quarter shareholder letter , and Hearst owns 18%.

Audiences are rewarding the bet. Monday Night Football drew its best Week 1 and Week 2 audiences ever this season. ABC’s September broadcast of Ohio State vs.…
items.t: Disney’s sports profit jumped 53% as it bets on live games. It also wants $3 billion in cost cuts

items.title: As attention spans move on from Iran and oil, the world is forever changed and the conflict is escalating again
items.summary:
The November news cycle has fixated on elections, Nvidia , and Anthropic, but the Iran war has quietly escalated this week and there is no “credible pathway” for the world to return to its previous norm, the International Energy Agency warned in its annual World Energy Outlook released Thursday.

Even as gasoline and diesel prices have fallen from record highs in recent weeks, the Middle East will never be the same and the rest of the world is still racing to develop more of its own energy sources—both renewables and fossil fuels—as global supplies remain tight and food security is threatened in much of the world, especially Asia, the report stated. All this is transpiring as global energy demand spikes both from the AI boom and the rise of the middle class in developing countries.

“While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be. And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said IEA executive director Fatih Birol.

The nearly nine-month Iran war and the prolonged shuttering of the vital Strait of Hormuz represent the greatest energy supply shock in modern history—far more than the Iranian Revolution or the Arab oil embargo of the 1970s—and its reverberations will be felt in ways that remain unclear, the report said. After all, the war is ongoing and Iran this week struck U.S. facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait, while the U.S. countered by striking Iran’s Qeshm Island.

“Attention is elsewhere now. I don’t know if it’s complacency…
items.t: As attention spans move on from Iran and oil, the world is forever changed and the conflict is escalating again

items.title: ‘Half philanthropy and half protest’: Noah Wyle and FIGS pair up to erase $200 million in real patients’ medical debt
items.summary:
After decades of playing a doctor on the long-running medical drama ER and today’s The Pitt, Noah Wyle has learned a thing or two about what it’s like to be a health care professional and the challenges patients face. 

Now, he is taking that passion off-screen, partnering up with popular scrubs maker FIGS with a goal to relieve at least $200 million of medical debt in the U.S. 

“In my countless interactions with healthcare professionals over the decades, one thing that stays with me is how they try to do everything right for a patient while the system makes it harder than it should be,” Wyle said in a statement. “Medical debt follows people home, creates long-term devastation, and changes the whole experience of care.”

Americans owe at least $220 billion in medical debt, according to a 2024 KFF-Peterson analysis of federal survey data, and having insurance offers less protection than many assume. In a new Urban Institute study backed by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, more than one-quarter of U.S. adults said they or a family member owed medical debt at the end of 2025, including 26% of those with health coverage. Hospitals were the most common creditor. 

Separately, a Commonwealth Fund survey released in September found that roughly one in three working-age adults with private insurance are paying off medical bills over time, with some pulling from savings or spending less on food and rent to keep up. The issue has also come up on screen in Wyle’s shows. In one episode of The Pitt , a construction worker who already owes $100,000 in medical bills lands in the ER…
items.t: ‘Half philanthropy and half protest’: Noah Wyle and FIGS pair up to erase $200 million in real patients’ medical debt

items.title: One in four boomers are still working well into their 70s because they can’t afford to retire—around 10% have even picked up second jobs
items.summary:
For years, turning 60 meant one thing: finally winding down and enjoying the fruits of your labor. But now a significant chunk of would-be retirees are working well into their 70s because they can’t afford to kick up their feet in the current economy.

In fact, more than one in four (27%) Americans aged 60 to 75 say they can’t afford to retire, according to a new snap poll by Resume Builder. Instead of going part-time and easing up, nearly 10% have found second jobs or additional income streams. And 12% who have already retired are now considering returning to work.

Unsurprisingly, it’s not because they miss the office. 

Among those still working, looking for work, or considering a return, 28% cite the high cost of living as their main reason—and it’s not because they were all financially reckless.

Most boomers have retirement savings—but they fear it won’t last 

Worryingly, nearly 20% of respondents admitted they have no retirement savings at all. But they’re in the minority. 

More than half of the respondents haven’t dipped into their retirement savings early, and just 15% say they haven’t saved enough for retirement. 

But prices keep climbing, and the nest egg they have now may not stretch to cover years —or rather, decades — of not working, especially if they want a retirement with holidays and the odd luxury, not just pottering around the house on the bare minimum.

Despite working for decades, 37% say they don’t have enough money to maintain an “acceptable standard of living” if they quit and retire right now.

It’s not just the current high cost of living…
items.t: One in four boomers are still working well into their 70s because they can’t afford to retire—around 10% have even picked up second jobs

items.title: Warby Parker is betting its next chapter on smart glasses people actually want to wear
items.summary:
Warby Parker is one of the clear winners of the 2010s-era direct-to-consumer (DTC) wave. It and other upstart digital-first brands like Allbirds shoes, Away luggage, and Casper mattresses used e-commerce savvy to cut out middlemen like wholesalers, upending their industries and selling straight to shoppers.

While many of its peers from that era have struggled or shut down, Warby Parker retains an empire of 360 stores; its revenue increased 10% to $245 million in its most recent quarter. Still, the eyewear company is grappling with soft growth in new active customers—only 3.4% last quarter—and a sluggish eyewear market overall.

In search of its next big growth engine, Warby Parker is planting its flag in the promising but still tiny market for smart glasses, teaming up with Google. The tech behemoth, along with partner Samsung , will provide the AI technology behind the glasses, including a high-resolution display tucked inside one lens that wearers can control with a wristband or watch.

For Warby Parker, whose own innovations have included a virtual try-on and features that enable customers to choose glasses from home, the partnership could bolster its tech-forward reputation, tapping its strengths in design and retail to win eyeglass buyers of the future.

“Glasses are the original wearable, right?” says Warby Parker co-founder and co-CEO Neil Blumenthal on Fortune ’s Behind the Business YouTube series. “The combination of form and function is something we can bring to this new category and create something that has a ton of technology in it.”

items.title: The world got used to endless Saudi cash. The Iran war ushered in a new reality
items.summary:
Head west out of Paris, and well-heeled suburbs give way to sleepy commuter towns. There, two dots on the map illustrate one of the most dizzying pipelines of wealth on the planet: Saudi Arabia. About 14 miles outside the capital sits Château Louis XIV, a close copy of the nearby real thing in Versailles; Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman bought the Château in 2015 for $300 million.

Turn north from there and you arrive at the small town of Cergy, where MBS inked a €6 billion deal in August to build three theme parks, apartment blocks, hotels, and infrastructure upgrades. “This project is designed to breathe new life into the territory,” Jean-Paul Jeandon, the area’s president, told me one rainy October evening. Without the Saudi deal, he said, Cergy faced poor growth prospects.

The town is not alone in tapping funds thousands of miles away—for good reason: For the past decade, the pool of Saudi money has seemed bottomless. With a steady influx of cash from vast oil reserves, the kingdom’s Public Investment Fund, or PIF—of which MBS is chairman—has seen its assets rocket 600% since 2015, to more than $900 billion, and has splurged on soccer , tech giants, California EV manufacturer Lucid, London’s Heathrow Airport, and numerous other investments, all while building mega-size tourism sites, arenas, and entertainment complexes back home.

Driving the action has been one defining project: Vision 2030, MBS’s signature strategy to transform the country by ending its overwhelming dependence on oil. No investment has seemed too big or costly; in fact, mammoth spending was…
items.t: The world got used to endless Saudi cash. The Iran war ushered in a new reality

items.title: Anthropic just set an IPO record nobody’s bragging about: $20 billion left on the table
items.summary:
The Anthropic IPO just delivered Wall Street’s AI bulls a strong vote of confidence. The Claude-purveyor’s big jump on its opening day of trading for now dispelled fears that investors’ faith in the profitability of this era’s signature technology was fading. 

Here’s an issue that the bulls are ignoring, and that’s getting virtually no coverage in the media: Anthropic left an enormous share of the IPO’s proceeds on the table. We’re talking about roughly $20 billion that could have flowed into spending on AI infrastructure that instead went to big institutions, and privileged retail investors, that reaped a gigantic, one-day windfall, as well as the underwriters that will feast on big commissions they’ll receive from the clients they awarded shares at what looks like bargain prices.

The “left on the table” phenomenon looks amazingly like the scenario surrounding the SpaceX debut in June, though all told, the Anthropic forgone funding number’s even bigger. So let’s start by comparing the two offerings. In total amount raised, Anthropic edged SpaceX as the biggest IPO of all time, collecting a headline, gross amount from the shares sold to the public of $81.34 billion versus $75 billion for SpaceX.

For additional insights into the similarities and contrasts between the two IPOs, I spoke to Jay Ritter, professor at the University of Florida and the world’s leading expert in the field. First, Ritter noted that the percentage fees paid the underwriters are the two lowest numbers he’s ever witnessed, chiefly because the deals are so immense that even at what sounds like a tiny…
items.t: Anthropic just set an IPO record nobody’s bragging about: $20 billion left on the table

items.title: Trump is one step closer to his ‘Golden Dome’ in Greenland, and it will be ‘absolutely devastating’ for U.S.-European relations
items.summary:
President Donald Trump is one step closer to his goal of expanding U.S. military presence across Greenland, but it may be costing America its relationship with Europe, long after Trump leaves the White House.

The Danish parliament unanimously approved a security deal with Trump on Thursday, which would allow the U.S. to have at least two additional military bases on Denmark’s autonomous territory of Greenland, as well as the construction of infrastructure for the “ Golden Dome ,” a multilayer missile defense system. Trump and the Danish and Greenlandic prime ministers initially signed the agreement in September. The pact still needs formal notification from the U.S. before it takes effect.

Trump has repeatedly threatened to take over Greenland since his second term began. He has argued that the country’s positioning between Russia and the U.S. creates the need for a strong American military presence to potentially track and intercept missiles. The island also is abundant in rare earths that have become more accessible as climate change melts the polar ice in the area.

Tensions between Trump and Denmark peaked in January, when the president refused to rule out military force in pursuit of the island, alarming not just Danish and Greenlandic authorities, but also longtime allies in NATO, especially because the U.S. and Denmark have had a longstanding defense agreement in place since 1951, which already outlines a path for the U.S. to grow and maintain a military presence on the island. Trump ruled out force days later, in a Jan. 21 speech at the World Economic Forum in…
items.t: Trump is one step closer to his ‘Golden Dome’ in Greenland, and it will be ‘absolutely devastating’ for U.S.-European relations

items.title: From losing it all to a $1 billion valuation: How Motorway’s CEO bounced back from failure
items.summary:
Tom Leathes and his two friends, Harry Jones and Alex Buttle were on a winning streak. Together, they built and sold office space platform Officila Space, broadband comparison site Top10.com, and LoanCube, a lead-generation site that was sold for $1 million. 

“We had this run of successes and thought we could do no wrong,” Leathes told Fortune. “And then we got quite schooled.” 

Their next business, a hotel recommendation app that kept the Top10 name, was their first to raise venture capital. It grew quickly, until Booking .com and the big hotel chains caught developed their own mobile apps. “All of the big hotel brands got mobile and killed us,” Leathes said. 

The founders spent two years trying to rescue the business, and a sale fell through at the last minute. They shut it down in 2015. “We lost all the money for the investors,” he said, referring to the $12.4 million the company had raised from backers including Balderton Capital and Accel. “We had to let go of the whole team.” The startup had 14 employees in London when it raised its last round in 2014. 

It was a “tough lesson,” Leathes admitted. The three went their separate ways, but within six months they were back together. “We had unfinished business,” he said. Their next venture, the trio agreed, had to be “the big one—the company that we can do for the next 10 or 20 years.” 

Leathes, Jones, and Buttle set about developing their next business idea from a disused hospital in Camden, north London, that was scheduled to be demolished. A charity had taken over the lease and was renting out the abandoned wards…

items.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
items.summary:
We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies

Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.

Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org
items.t: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras

When the Dublin-born writer Walsh finally appeared, Boyle introduced himself. He was from west Belfast, he’d read Walsh’s plays at drama school, and it was his dream to work with him one day. He asked if Walsh would like to come and see him on Broadway, where he was playing Scorpius Malfoy, son of Draco, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. How did he respond? Boyle grins. “He was sort of like: ‘Oh.’”

items.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
items.summary:
He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
items.summary:
It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year

  • Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166

The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January. But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving.

Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use.

items.t: Energy price cap rise: how to beat the January hike

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.
